1. Introduction
The increasing energy demand, and vastly depleting fossil fuels are 
the two main reasons to create the research interest towards clean, 
green, and renewable energy sources for energy production and storage. 
In the last few decades, fuel cells and batteries have played a major role 
in our earth's indispensable energy requirements but the two funda -
mental components of systems that continuously store and distribute 
energy are traditional capacitors and batteries. Batteries, on the other 
hand, provide a substantial amount of energy with low power density, 
whereas ordinary capacitors have no energy density but provide high 
power density [ 1 – 5 ]. As a result, attention to evolve the improved high- 
power, and high-energy density energy storage devices has been focused 
by many researchers [ 6 , 7 ].
Supercapacitors (SCs) are one kind of energy storage system that has 
captivated a lot of scientific interest today. Supercapacitors have two 
distinct methods of storing energy: electrical double-layer capacitance 
(EDLC) and pseudocapacitance. Carbonaceous materials with excess 
conductivity and high surface areas like activated carbon (AC), gra -
phene, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are known as EDLC electrode 
materials [ 8 , 9 ]. On the other side, metal oxides, carbides, nitrides, sel -
enides, and conducting polymers undergo reversible redox reactions 
which are pseudocapacitive electrode materials because of their abun -
dance in nature, cost-effectiveness, and extraordinary capacity to store

In this work, we report for the first time according to our under -
standing the synthesis of a novel nanocomposite comprising nickel 
nanoparticles, multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), and activated 
carbon derived from Conocarpus tree bark (CTB-AC), highlighting a 
unique combination of materials. The use of biomass-derived activated 
carbon introduces a sustainable and cost-effective material, aligning 
with green chemistry principles and offering an eco-friendly alternative 
to conventional materials. A simple yet scalable ultrasonic-assisted 
method was employed to achieve a well-integrated structure, wherein 
CTB-based activated carbon enhances the surface area of MWCNTs, and 
Ni incorporation significantly boosts electrochemical performance. The 
resulting Ni@MWCNT/CTB-AC composite exhibited exceptional spe -
cific capacitance, rate capability, and cyclic stability, attributed to its 
unique structural synergy. Furthermore, the binder-free device fabri -
cated from this composite showcased excellent mechanical robustness 
and successfully powered a blue LED, demonstrating practical applica -
tion potential. This innovative approach introduces a new class of hybrid 
nanomaterials while advancing sustainable energy storage through the 
valorization of waste-derived biomass. By utilizing CTB, the work sup -
ports clean energy solutions and contributes to the global transition 
away from fossil fuels.

4.2. Powering of blue LED using Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB
The flexible devices are connected either in series or in parallel to 
satisfy the necessary energy/power constraint to assess the constructed 
Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB's practical functionality. To demonstrate the 
adaptability of our ASC devices in both topologies, four devices were 
coupled in series and parallel ( Fig. 10 ). Surprisingly, compared to a 
single ASC device with an operating potential window of 0.8 V, the four 
serially connected devices generated a 3.2 V CV curve and a GCD po -
tential window with a comparable discharge duration. The CV results 
( Fig. 10 a and Fig. 10 b) and the GCD results ( Fig. 10 c and Fig. 10 d) of the 
Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB fabricated electrodes in series and parallel con -
nections are demonstrated in the figures. Four devices could instantly 
power LEDs (blue) for longer than 5 min using the series connection 
( Fig. 10 e and Fig. 10 f). As a result, the Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB asym -
metric hybrid flexible supercapacitor is likely to find an outlet in the 
green energy industry.
5. Conclusion
AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC were employed to create an 
innovative nanocomposite towards flexible asymmetric supercapacitor 
applications. Electrochemical, elemental, structural, and morphological 
characterizations were performed for the produced nanocomposite. The 
SEM image reveals that the AC-CTB structure is highly porous, enabling 
greater loading of MWCNTs and Ni nanoparticles, while also enhancing 
ion adsorption and desorption during charge – discharge cycles. In 1 M
